questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Show how the following have been used to group crystals into different systems:

(i) Crystallographic axes and axial angles;

(ii) Diagnostic symmetry elements.

(14 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Crystals are grouped into **seven crystal systems** (some books use six, with the trigonal system placed in the hexagonal one). The grouping rests on two sets of facts: **(i) the crystallographic axes and the angles between them**, and **(ii) the symmetry elements** (planes, axes and centre of symmetry) which the crystals possess.

**(i) Crystallographic axes and axial angles.** The crystal faces are referred to imaginary lines through the centre of the crystal, the **crystallographic axes** ($a$, $b$, $c$; and $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$ and $c$ in the hexagonal system), which are parallel to the main edges. $\alpha$ is the angle between $b$ and $c$, $\beta$ between $a$ and $c$, and $\gamma$ between $a$ and $b$. The systems differ in **the number of axes, the relative lengths of the axes and the angles between them**:

| System | Axes (lengths) | Axial angles | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cubic** (isometric) | three equal: $a = b = c$ | $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90°$ | halite, galena, pyrite, fluorite, garnet |
| **Tetragonal** | two equal, one different: $a = b \neq c$ | $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90°$ | zircon, rutile, cassiterite |
| **Orthorhombic** | three unequal: $a \neq b \neq c$ | $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90°$ | olivine, barite, topaz, sulphur |
| **Monoclinic** | three unequal: $a \neq b \neq c$ | $\alpha = \gamma = 90°$, $\beta \neq 90°$ | gypsum, orthoclase, augite, mica |
| **Triclinic** | three unequal: $a \neq b \neq c$ | $\alpha \neq \beta \neq \gamma$, none equal to $90°$ | plagioclase feldspar, kyanite |
| **Hexagonal** | four axes: three equal ones in one plane, $a_1 = a_2 = a_3 \neq c$ | $a$-axes at $120°$ to each other, $c$ at $90°$ to the plane of the $a$-axes | beryl, apatite |
| **Trigonal** (rhombohedral) | as hexagonal ($a_1 = a_2 = a_3 \neq c$), or three equal axes $a = b = c$ with equal angles | $\alpha = \beta = \gamma \neq 90°$ in rhombohedral axes | quartz, calcite |

**(ii) Diagnostic symmetry elements.** There are three types of symmetry elements: a **plane of symmetry** (a mirror plane which divides the crystal into two halves which are mirror images), an **axis of symmetry** (a line about which the crystal is rotated through $360°$ and repeats its appearance 2, 3, 4 or 6 times: a diad, triad, tetrad or hexad) and a **centre of symmetry** (every face has an equal and parallel face opposite). The element that **defines** each system is:

| System | Diagnostic (essential) symmetry element | Total in the highest symmetry class |
|---|---|---|
| Cubic | **four 3-fold axes** (along the body diagonals) | 9 planes, 13 axes, 1 centre (23 elements) |
| Tetragonal | **one 4-fold axis** (along $c$) | 5 planes, 5 axes, 1 centre (11 elements) |
| Orthorhombic | **three mutually perpendicular 2-fold axes** (or 2-fold axes and planes) | 3 planes, 3 axes, 1 centre (7 elements) |
| Monoclinic | **one 2-fold axis** (or one plane of symmetry) | 1 plane, 1 axis, 1 centre (3 elements) |
| Triclinic | **no axis or plane**; at most a centre of symmetry | 0 planes, 0 axes, 1 centre (1 element) |
| Hexagonal | **one 6-fold axis** (along $c$) | 7 planes, 7 axes, 1 centre (15 elements) |
| Trigonal | **one 3-fold axis** (along $c$) | 3 planes, 4 axes, 1 centre (8 elements) |

So a crystal is put in the system with the same **axial scheme and the same essential symmetry element**: the simple relations of the axes are a result of the symmetry. (Neat sketches of the axial cross for the cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic and hexagonal systems, with the angles marked, are credited.)

The **pyroxenes** are a group of rock-forming, **ferromagnesian silicate** minerals with the general formula $\mathrm{XY(Si,Al)_2O_6}$, where X is Ca, Na, Fe$^{2+}$ or Mg and Y is Mg, Fe or Al. They are important minerals of basic and ultrabasic igneous rocks.

**(i) Structure (about 4 marks).** The pyroxenes are **single-chain silicates (inosilicates)**. Each $\mathrm{SiO_4}$ tetrahedron **shares two of its four oxygens** with the next tetrahedra, forming long, **single chains** with the repeat unit $\mathrm{(SiO_3)^{2-}}$ (the ratio of Si to O is 1 to 3). The chains run parallel to the $c$ axis and are **held together by the cations** (Mg, Fe, Ca, Na, Al) located between them, in sites M1 and M2. The bonds between chains (ionic) are weaker than the bonds inside the chains (Si-O), so the minerals have **two directions of cleavage parallel to the chains**. Substitution of Mg for Fe, and Ca, Na and Al, gives a range of compositions: **enstatite** $\mathrm{MgSiO_3}$ and hypersthene (**orthopyroxenes**), and **diopside**, **augite**, hedenbergite, jadeite and aegirine (**clinopyroxenes**).

**(ii) Crystallography (about 3 marks).**

- The **orthopyroxenes** (enstatite, hypersthene) crystallise in the **orthorhombic system**, and the **clinopyroxenes** (diopside, augite, jadeite, aegirine, spodumene) in the **monoclinic system**.
- Crystals are **short, stout prisms** with a nearly **square or eight-sided (octagonal) cross-section**; they are commonly in grains or granular masses, and are rarely well formed in rocks. Simple and polysynthetic **twinning** is found in augite and in diopside.

**(iii) Diagnostic physical properties (about 4 marks).**

- **Colour:** usually **green, dark green, brown or black** (augite is black or dark green, diopside pale to dark green, enstatite grey, greenish or brown, jadeite green or white, aegirine black or dark green).
- **Lustre:** vitreous to dull; **streak** white to grey or pale green.
- **Cleavage:** **two good cleavages, nearly at right angles** (about 87° and 93°), parallel to the chains. This is the property that **separates pyroxene from amphibole**, which has cleavages at about 56° and 124°.
- **Hardness:** about **5 to 6** on Mohs' scale; **specific gravity** about **3.2 to 3.6**; fracture uneven to conchoidal, and brittle.
- **Occurrence:** in **basic and ultrabasic igneous rocks** (gabbro, basalt, dolerite, peridotite), and in high-grade metamorphic rocks (granulite, eclogite with omphacite). Pyroxene **alters** to amphibole (uralite), chlorite or serpentine, and it is not found with quartz in a rock in large amounts (in agreement with Bowen's series).
